opus-5.5.text:
I think the application should come first, and then you ask what kind of capability it actually demands. People often frame pre-training versus RL as a technical debate, but the right answer depends heavily on what you want the agent to do.

If the application needs broad general knowledge, common sense, language understanding, the ability to handle the long tail of situations nobody anticipated, then pre-training does most of the heavy lifting. It's the source of priors. RL can't create those from scratch efficiently, because the exploration space is too big and the reward too sparse. Pre-training gives you a policy that already does something reasonable, so RL has somewhere to start.

But if the application has a clear notion of success, like writing code that passes tests, solving a math problem, or completing a web task, then RL becomes very powerful, because you can define a reward and let the model improve beyond what imitating human data gives you. Human data tells you what people did, not necessarily what's optimal. Especially for agents acting over many steps, the model needs to learn from its own trajectories and mistakes, and that's what RL does well.

So my view is that it isn't really an either-or. Pre-training builds the prior, RL aligns that prior to a particular environment and objective. What's changed recently is that the bottleneck has shifted. A few years ago the question was whether the model was smart enough. Now the model is quite capable, and the harder question is what environments and tasks we should define, and what reward actually captures value for the user. In a sense, the application defines the environment, and the environment defines what RL can teach.

One more point. Many real applications don't have clean rewards. Helping someone with research, being a good assistant over months, doing a job in a company. The reward is fuzzy, delayed, sometimes subjective. For those, you can't just turn the RL crank. You need good priors, good evaluation, maybe memory and interaction with the user over time. I think that's where a lot of the interesting work is going to be: figuring out how to turn messy real-world utility into something models can learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says RL can be powerful for narrow tasks with clear rewards and learning from agent trajectories, but it does not say that abundant data and a trustworthy closed learning loop make a primarily RL-based agent sufficient.

r002.rationale: The response says pre-training supplies broad priors for handling the long tail of situations nobody anticipated, directly linking it to generalization beyond familiar cases.

r003.rationale: The response discusses applications, rewards, and user value, but does not identify value exceeding cost as the condition for accepting an approach.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the application decides what counts as a "task," and once you know what the task is, the division of labor between pre-training and RL kind of falls out naturally.

Pre-training gives you priors. It gives you a model that knows language, knows code, knows how the world roughly works, has read all the documentation and all the Stack Overflow answers. That's incredibly valuable, but it's passive knowledge. It doesn't tell the model what to do when it's in an environment, takes an action, and the environment pushes back in a way it didn't expect. RL is how you turn priors into behavior. It's how the model learns from the consequences of its own actions rather than from what someone else wrote down.

So the question I'd ask about any agent application is: how much of the difficulty is in the prior, and how much is in the feedback loop? If you're building a coding agent, a lot of the hard part is already in pre-training, because there's an enormous amount of code and reasoning about code on the internet. What RL adds is the ability to run the tests, see the failure, and recover. That's a relatively tight loop with a clear reward, so RL works really well there, and we've seen that. On the other hand, if you're building something like a web agent or a computer-use agent, the prior is much weaker. There's not much text on the internet about "here's what I clicked, here's what happened, here's what I should have clicked instead." So you end up needing a lot more environment interaction, and the environment itself becomes the bottleneck, not the algorithm.

That's actually my bigger point. I think for a long time the field was algorithm-driven, and now it's becoming environment-driven. Pre-training was about scaling data; RL for agents is about scaling environments and tasks. If you ask me where the leverage is for a specific application, I'd say it's less about picking pre-training versus RL and more about: can you build an environment that faithfully represents the real task, with a reward signal you actually trust? If yes, RL will get you a long way. If no, you're mostly relying on the prior, and you should spend your effort on data and on designing the agent's interface, things like what tools it has, how it represents memory, how it decomposes the problem. ReAct, for example, didn't require any training at all. It was just a better way to use the prior.

The other thing I'd say is that generalization across tasks is still the open question. Pre-training generalizes beautifully because the data is so diverse. RL on a narrow set of tasks tends to give you a model that's great at those tasks and brittle elsewhere. So if your application is narrow, say one company's internal workflow, you can go heavy on RL and it's fine. If your application is "a general assistant that does anything on a computer," you need RL over a very diverse distribution of tasks, and at that point it starts to look a lot like pre-training again, just with actions and feedback instead of next tokens. I actually think that's where things converge. The distinction between the two phases is going to get blurrier, and what remains is the question of where the signal comes from: from humans writing things down, or from the agent trying things in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says a narrow application can go heavy on RL and describes clear feedback loops, but it does not state that abundant data is available or that the application is valuable.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training generalizes broadly and that agents meant to handle diverse tasks need diverse training, supporting the role of pre-training for generalization beyond familiar tasks.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify whether an agent’s value exceeds its cost as the deciding condition for an acceptable technical approach.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with what you want the agent to do. What environment will it operate in? What actions can it take? And how will you know whether it succeeded? Those questions should guide the choice between pre-training and reinforcement learning.

Pre-training gives you a broad foundation: knowledge, language understanding, and patterns you can learn from existing data. But an agent also needs to make decisions and deal with the consequences. If the application has an environment where you can practice and get reliable feedback—for example, a coding agent that can run tests—then reinforcement learning becomes particularly useful. You can train on whether the agent actually solves the task, rather than just whether its next response looks plausible.

If feedback is ambiguous, or interacting with the environment is expensive, then it’s harder to make reinforcement learning effective. You might initially get more value from better pre-training data or demonstrations.

So I wouldn’t treat this as choosing one over the other. The application tells you what capabilities you need, which ones the model already has, and what you can improve through interaction. That determines where you should invest.

r001.rationale: It says reliable environmental feedback can make reinforcement learning useful, but does not suggest that a primarily RL-based agent could suffice for a narrow application with abundant data and a trustworthy learning loop.

r002.rationale: It describes pre-training as a broad foundation, but does not connect its importance to generalizing to unfamiliar environments or tasks.

r003.rationale: It notes that expensive or ambiguous feedback can make RL harder, but does not state that an agent’s value exceeding its cost determines whether its technical approach is acceptable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with what you want the agent to do. What environment will it operate in? What feedback can you get? How expensive is it to try something and find out whether it worked? Those questions should shape the training approach.

If the application requires broad knowledge and the ability to handle many different situations, pre-training provides that foundation. But if you have a specific task where the agent can interact with an environment and receive reliable feedback, reinforcement learning becomes very useful. It can learn not just to produce a plausible answer, but to take actions that lead to a successful outcome.

For example, in a coding application, you can often run tests and check whether a change works. That gives you a fairly concrete training signal. For a more open-ended assistant, success may be much harder to measure. If you optimize a narrow proxy, you can get better scores without actually making the assistant more useful.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one universally over the other. Pre-training gives you a starting point, and reinforcement learning lets you improve behavior through experience. The application determines what experience you can collect and what feedback you can trust—and that determines where reinforcement learning will help.

r001.rationale: The response says RL is useful for specific tasks with reliable feedback, but does not say it may suffice as the primary approach or mention abundant data.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training supports broad knowledge and many situations, but does not identify generalization to unfamiliar environments or tasks.

r003.rationale: It mentions the cost of trying actions as a factor in training choices, but does not make value exceeding cost the condition for an acceptable technical approach.
